name: Mental Maths: Squares Ending in 5
description: A KaTeX-enabled deck for the high-value square-ending-in-5 method. It covers the algebraic reason behind the shortcut, two- to four-digit examples, reverse recognition, common traps, estimation, and mixed mastery practice.
estimatedTime: 130–170 minutes for a first focused pass; then 10–15 minute review bursts

cards.term: Squares Ending in 5: What is the core rule?
cards.definition:
For a number ending in 5, multiply the digits before 5 by the next integer, then append 25.

$$
\begin{aligned}
85^2 \\
8\times9&=72 \\
85^2&=7225
\end{aligned}
$$

cards.term: Squares Ending in 5: Why does the rule work?
cards.definition:
Let the number be 10a + 5.

$$
\begin{aligned}
(10a+5)^2 \\
&=100a^2+100a+25 \\
&=100a(a+1)+25
\end{aligned}
$$
So compute a(a + 1), then append 25.

cards.term: Squares Ending in 5: Does the rule work beyond two digits?
cards.definition:
Yes. For 125², take 12 and multiply by 13, then append 25.

$$
\begin{aligned}
125^2 \\
12\times13&=156 \\
125^2&=15625
\end{aligned}
$$

cards.term: Squares Ending in 5: What does “append 25” mean?
cards.definition:
It means the result always ends in 25.

For 65², 6 × 7 = 42, so the answer is 4225, not 42 + 25 = 67.

cards.term: Squares Ending in 5: Which method is best for 95²?
cards.definition:
Use the ending-in-5 rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}
95^2 \\
9\times10&=90 \\
95^2&=9025
\end{aligned}
$$

cards.term: Squares Ending in 5: Which method is best for 235²?
cards.definition:
Use the ending-in-5 rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}
235^2 \\
23\times24&=552 \\
235^2&=55225
\end{aligned}
$$

cards.term: Squares Ending in 5: How can you estimate the answer?
cards.definition:
A number near 100 squared is near 10,000; a number near 200 squared is near 40,000. This catches misplaced zeros.

Example: 195² must be near 200² = 40000; exact result 38025.

cards.term: Squares Ending in 5: What is the last-digit check?
cards.definition: Every integer ending in 5 has a square ending in 25. Any other ending indicates an error.

cards.term: Squares Ending in 5: When should you not use this rule?
cards.definition: Only use it for numbers ending exactly in 5. For 84², choose a near-base or expansion method instead.
Take 1 and multiply by 2, then append 25: 15² = 225.

Take 100 and multiply by 101, then append 25.

100 × 101 = 10100, so 1005² = 1010025.

cards.term: Squares Ending in 5: How does the rule connect to consecutive products?
cards.definition: The digits before 5 always form a consecutive product: a(a + 1). This is why the square-ending-5 method also strengthens multiplication fluency.

cards.term: Can a number ending in 5 have a square ending in 75?
cards.definition: No. The square must end in 25.
Ending-in-5 rule: 7 × 8 = 56, then append 25, giving 5625.
Not the ending-in-5 rule. Use a near-base method such as (80 + 4)² or (100 − 16)².

cards.term: True or false: The ending-in-5 rule works for 1005².
cards.definition: True. The prefix is 100; calculate 100 × 101, then append 25.

cards.term: True or false: Append 25 means add 25 to the consecutive product.
cards.definition: False. It means write 25 as the final two digits.
